agenda: Maintenance of international peace and security: Climate and security
cosponsors: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: Estonia’s objective is to secure a pragmatic, implementable climate-security text that mainstreams risk assessment into existing UN conflict-prevention and reporting tools while reaffirming UNFCCC primacy, national circumstances and no new legal obligations. The main difficulty is Russia’s opposition to any Security Council role on climate, with India and China also wary of creating a formal security link; the text therefore explicitly avoids Article 39 determinations, Chapter VII and automatic sanctions or force to prevent a veto. Estonia will still seek to retain the Secretary-General reporting and risk-integration language during negotiations, while working to keep at least nine positive votes.

China.change: Add: 'Reaffirming the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances, as enshrined in the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement;'

Replace 'Welcoming the work of the United Nations Climate Security Mechanism and noting the need for enhanced coordination and information-sharing across the United Nations system' with 'Noting the need for enhanced coordination and information-sharing across the United Nations system, within existing mandates and resources and without prejudice to the mandates of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement;'
Delete 'including through the United Nations Climate Security Mechanism' and insert 'within existing mandates and resources and in full respect of the mandates of relevant United Nations entities'

Replace 'Requests the Secretary-General' with 'Invites the Secretary-General' and add 'in full respect of the mandates of the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and without creating new reporting obligations'
Add 'in accordance with the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, including the obligations of developed countries to provide and mobilize climate finance to developing countries'

France.change: Replace with: 'Recognizing that the adverse effects of climate change can act as a threat multiplier and can pose risks to international peace and security;'

Replace 'integrate climate-related security risk assessment and risk management, as appropriate, into' with 'systematically integrate climate-related security risk assessment and risk management into'

Replace 'provide, within existing resources and as appropriate, information and analysis' with 'provide, within existing resources, regular information and analysis'; and replace 'including by incorporating such risks, where relevant, in regular reporting and briefings' with 'including by systematically incorporating such risks in regular reporting and briefings'

India.change: Delete OP3 in its entirety. The Security Council must not direct the Secretary-General to integrate climate-related security risk assessment and risk management into United Nations conflict prevention, early warning, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding strategies.

Delete OP4 in its entirety. The Council should not request information and analysis on climate-related security risks in situations on its agenda, as this duplicates the UNFCCC and other United Nations bodies.
Delete the paragraph on climate finance. Climate finance is negotiated under the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and the Security Council should not address it.
Delete the invitation for an oral briefing by December 2022 on implementation, or make it a voluntary informational briefing without follow-up obligations.

Add a preambular paragraph: 'Reaffirming the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances, and that climate action must be pursued through the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement.'

Kenya.change: Add ', including in Africa, particularly the Sahel and the Horn of Africa' after 'humanitarian crises'.
Replace 'relevant regional organizations' with 'relevant regional and subregional organizations, including the African Union'.

Replace OP7 with: 'Emphasizes the importance of scaled-up, predictable, adequate and accessible climate finance, including for adaptation and resilience, in conflict-affected and fragile contexts, in particular in Africa, and encourages Member States and relevant institutions to consider ways to enhance access to such finance, including through simplified procedures, while avoiding the diversion of resources from development and peacekeeping activities;'

Russian Federation.change: Replace with: 'Invites the Secretary-General, within existing mandates and resources, in consultation with Member States and relevant regional organizations, and with the consent of the affected Member State, to consider climate-related security risks, as appropriate, in United Nations conflict prevention, early warning, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding efforts, without creating new mandates or structures and without prejudice to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change;'

Replace with: 'Invites the Secretary-General, in consultation with the affected Member State and respecting the mandates of other United Nations entities, to provide, as appropriate and within existing resources, information on climate-related security risks in situations on the Council’s agenda, without creating an automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions;'

Replace 'Invites the Secretary-General to provide an oral briefing to the Council by December 2022, within existing resources, on the implementation of the present resolution, including challenges and good practices;' with 'Invites the Secretary-General to provide, on a voluntary basis and in consultation with Member States, an oral briefing to the Council by December 2022, within existing resources, on the implementation of the present resolution, including challenges and good practices;'

Replace with: 'Encourages Member States and relevant institutions, in relevant international forums, to consider ways to enhance access to climate finance in conflict-affected and fragile contexts, while avoiding the diversion of resources from development and peacekeeping activities, and reaffirms that the present resolution does not create new financial obligations;'

Add new preambular paragraph: 'Reaffirming that the present resolution does not create a new thematic agenda item or mandate for the Security Council and should not lead to the securitization of climate change, which is addressed under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement;'

Viet Nam.change: Insert “sea-level rise and saltwater intrusion,” after “including through”, so that the paragraph reads: “...including through sea-level rise and saltwater intrusion, water and food insecurity, displacement, competition over natural resources and loss of livelihoods...”
Insert “and in close consultation with the concerned Member States” after “as appropriate,” so that reporting is undertaken with their views taken into account.

messages.China: China supports the Council's consideration of climate-related risks but stresses that climate change is primarily a development issue and that the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement are the primary forums. We can support the draft if it explicitly reaffirms common but differentiated responsibilities and avoids endorsing the Climate Security Mechanism or creating new reporting mandates. We ask the penholder to incorporate these changes to ensure the text remains within existing mandates and respects the division of labor across the UN system.
messages.France: France strongly supports the objective of this resolution and commends Estonia for advancing it. We would like the text to retain the recognition that climate change can act as a threat multiplier and to strengthen the operational follow-up through more systematic risk integration and reporting, while preserving the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement as the primary forums and avoiding new legal obligations.
messages.India: India appreciates the effort to include safeguards, but the current text still operationalizes a climate-security link through OP3, OP4 and OP9. We cannot support a resolution that asks the Secretary-General to integrate climate-related security risk assessment into Council-mandated work or to report on climate risks in agenda situations, as this duplicates and prejudges the UNFCCC. Our red lines are deletion of OP3 and OP4; we also need OP7 and OP9 removed or recast and an explicit CBDR reaffirmation.
messages.Ireland: Ireland supports the draft as a carefully balanced compromise and, as a co-sponsor, does not propose amendments at this stage. We urge all Council members to support swift adoption and to avoid reopening agreed language. Ireland remains ready to discuss implementation, including strengthening climate-related security risk assessment within existing mandates.
messages.Kenya: Kenya supports the draft's core objective and the recognition that climate change can be a risk multiplier. We ask the penholder to reflect more explicitly the disproportionate impact on Africa, particularly the Sahel and Horn of Africa, and to name the African Union in coordination provisions. We also seek stronger language on scaled-up and accessible climate finance for adaptation and resilience in conflict-affected and fragile contexts, including in Africa. Kenya can support the text with these improvements.
messages.Mexico: Mexico co-sponsored this draft and supports it as a balanced compromise that recognizes climate-related risks while respecting the primacy of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement and avoiding new obligations. We welcome the safeguards on national circumstances, existing mandates and resources, and conflict-sensitive approaches. Mexico encourages all Council members to join consensus so the Council can act on climate and security.
messages.Niger: Niger is a co-sponsor of this balanced draft and strongly supports its adoption. As a Sahelian country confronting desertification, food insecurity and the Lake Chad crisis, we view climate-related security risks as a real risk multiplier and urge Council members to preserve the agreed compromise language. We should avoid reopening the text and send a unified signal on climate and security.
messages.Norway: Norway fully supports the draft as a carefully balanced compromise that recognizes climate-related security risks while respecting the mandates of the UNFCCC and other UN bodies. As a co-sponsor, we urge all Council members to support the text as it stands and to avoid reopening language that could undermine consensus.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation views the revised text as a basis for consensus, but we cannot accept operative paragraphs 3 and 4 in their current form as they risk creating a de facto climate-security reporting mandate. We propose replacing 'Requests' with 'Invites', ensuring the consent of the affected Member State, and explicitly reaffirming that this does not create a new thematic agenda or mandate. We also seek amendments to OP9 to make the briefing voluntary and to OP7 to clarify that no new financial obligations are created.
messages.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines thanks Estonia for its efforts and supports the draft as a carefully balanced compromise, which we are pleased to co-sponsor. We underscore that for small island developing States, climate change and sea-level rise are existential threats, and we value the text's recognition of climate-related security risks. We therefore urge delegations not to reopen the text and call for its adoption.
messages.Tunisia: Tunisia thanks Estonia for its work and confirms its co-sponsorship of the current text. We support the balanced language reaffirming the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement as the primary forums while recognizing climate-related risks to peace and security, including in Africa and fragile contexts. We have no changes to request at this stage and encourage the Council to maintain this consensus text.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom is a co-sponsor of this balanced text and supports its adoption as it stands. It reflects a carefully negotiated compromise that keeps UNFCCC primacy while enabling the Council to integrate climate-related security risks into its work. We urge all Council members to join consensus and send a unified message on climate and security.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports the current text as a balanced and practical basis for Council action. It preserves the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement as the primary forums, respects existing mandates and resources, and appropriately recognizes climate-related risks as a risk multiplier in conflict prevention and reporting. We urge all Council members to join consensus and move this draft to a vote without weakening its operational provisions.
messages.Viet Nam: Viet Nam supports the balanced and carefully calibrated draft, in particular its reaffirmation of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement and its safeguards against creating new obligations. We ask that OP1 expressly include sea-level rise and saltwater intrusion among the adverse effects that can exacerbate existing challenges, reflecting the existential risks to low-lying coastal States and deltas. We also ask that OP4 be carried out in close consultation with concerned Member States, consistent with national ownership and non-intervention. These targeted changes would strengthen the text without reopening its core balance.

replies.China: partially accepted: CBDR and safeguards accepted; CSM reference removed and reporting softened, but explicit developed-country finance obligation not added.
replies.France: partially accepted: threat-multiplier language retained, but operational integration softened to avoid new mandates.
replies.India: rejected: OP3 and OP4 retained in weakened form; OP7 retained; OP9 made voluntary.
replies.Kenya: partially accepted: Africa, Sahel, Horn of Africa and African Union references added, with strengthened finance language but no new obligations.
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: OP3 and OP4 recast as invitations with consent and no new mandates, OP9 made voluntary, OP7 includes no new financial obligations, and a new preambular paragraph added.
replies.United States of America: partially accepted: risk and information-analysis language retained, but operational provisions recast to avoid new reporting obligations.
replies.Viet Nam: accepted: sea-level rise and saltwater intrusion added to OP1; OP4 includes close consultation with concerned Member States.

steps.summary: The revised text accommodates China's CBDR red line and Russia's OP3 and OP4 red lines by converting operational requests into invitations with consent and no new mandates, while retaining climate-security risk language and targeted African, finance and sea-level-rise references. Estonia expects broad support, with India likely opposed and one possible abstention, but no P5 veto.

messages.China: China welcomes the incorporation of CBDR and the safeguards against securitization, new mandates and automatic linkages. We still request that OP7 explicitly reflect the obligations of developed countries to provide and mobilize climate finance to developing countries, in accordance with the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. With this addition, China is prepared to support the text.
messages.France: France thanks Estonia for retaining the threat-multiplier language and can support the balance safeguarding UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. To make the text operationally credible, we need OP3 and OP4 to require systematic integration and regular risk information within existing mandates and resources, not optional 'as appropriate' language. France also asks to remove the preambular disclaimer that undercuts the Council's recognition of climate-related security risks, while keeping the existing conflict-risk language.
messages.India: India cannot support the current text because OP3 and OP4 still invite the Secretary-General to integrate climate-related security risks into the Council’s conflict-prevention work and to provide climate-security analysis on agenda situations. These provisions cross our red lines and risk securitizing climate change, which must remain within the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. We also ask that OP7 be deleted or replaced, since climate finance belongs in the UNFCCC process. Unless OP3 and OP4 are removed, India will vote against the draft.
messages.Ireland: Ireland supports the current text as a balanced and carefully negotiated compromise. We thank the penholder and all co-sponsors, and we urge the Council to adopt it without further amendment so that the Council can begin integrating climate-related security risks into its conflict prevention and peacebuilding work, within existing mandates and in full respect of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement.
messages.Kenya: Kenya supports the current text as a balanced compromise that reflects key African priorities, including explicit references to Africa, the Sahel and the Horn of Africa, the African Union, and accessible climate finance for conflict-affected and fragile contexts. We appreciate the penholder’s efforts to incorporate these concerns while preserving the centrality of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. Kenya encourages all Council members to unite behind the draft and calls for its adoption.
messages.Mexico: Mexico supports the current draft as a balanced and carefully calibrated text. It reaffirms the centrality of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, respects national circumstances and avoids creating new obligations or mandates, while allowing the Council to consider climate-related risks within existing mandates. As a co-sponsor, Mexico urges the Council to adopt the text without further changes and to ensure its inclusive and conflict-sensitive implementation.
messages.Niger: Niger supports the current text and commends the penholder for a balanced, consensus-oriented draft. As a Sahelian State and co-sponsor, we welcome the references to the Sahel, climate finance for Africa, African Union consultation, national ownership and the primacy of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. We have no further changes and call for the Council to adopt the text.
messages.Norway: Norway supports the current draft as a balanced compromise and welcomes its broad co-sponsorship. It reflects key Norwegian priorities by recognising climate-related risks as a threat multiplier while reaffirming the primacy of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. Norway urges all Council members to support the text and avoid reopening delicate compromises.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation acknowledges the progress in revision 1, particularly the new preambular paragraph and the voluntary nature of the briefing. However, OP4 still refers to 'information and analysis' and 'concerned Member States' without grounding the provision in consultation with the affected Member State. We cannot support the text unless OP4 is revised as proposed to ensure information only, without analysis, and in consultation with the affected State.
messages.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines thanks the penholder and supports the current text. As a small island developing State, we believe it appropriately captures the security implications of sea-level rise and climate impacts while preserving UNFCCC primacy and avoiding new obligations. We urge all Council members to support its adoption.
messages.Tunisia: Tunisia thanks Estonia for the balanced revision and confirms its support for the current text. As a co-sponsor, we believe the safeguards on sovereignty, CBDR, and the primacy of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, together with the focus on Africa and conflict-affected contexts, address our key concerns. We have no further changes and encourage the Council to proceed to a vote.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom welcomes the balanced and consensus-oriented text and thanks Estonia for its work. We are pleased to co-sponsor this resolution and support its adoption. We encourage all Council members to unite behind it.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports the revised draft and urges all Council members to vote in favor. This balanced text appropriately recognizes climate-related security risks while reaffirming the central role of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement and respecting existing mandates and resources. We see no need for further changes and call for its adoption.
messages.Viet Nam: Viet Nam thanks the penholder for accepting our proposals on OP1 and OP4. The current text reflects a careful balance by recognizing sea-level rise and saltwater intrusion, reaffirming the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement as the primary forums, upholding CBDR, and avoiding new mandates or an automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions. Viet Nam supports the text as it stands and encourages the Council to maintain this balanced approach.

reasons.China: China’s established position opposes Security Council securitization of climate change and insists on UNFCCC primacy; the actual 13 Dec 2021 resolution saw China abstain despite watered-down language. The accepted OP7 language does not overcome those broader principled concerns.
reasons.Estonia: As the submitting delegation, Estonia supports the balanced text and its safeguards for UNFCCC primacy, national ownership and existing mandates. It will vote yes and explain support before adoption.
reasons.France: France strongly supports the climate-security agenda and, despite a watered-down text and only partial acceptance of its amendments, the resolution still advances risk integration while preserving UNFCCC safeguards, so France would vote yes.
reasons.India: India had already opposed the draft and its red lines on OP3 and OP4 were rejected; voting against follows its longstanding position that climate change should remain within UNFCCC/Paris processes rather than be securitized by the Security Council.
reasons.Ireland: Ireland is listed as a co-sponsor, made no requested changes, and supports integrating climate-related security risk assessment while preserving UNFCCC primacy and existing mandates. Its foreign policy priorities on conflict prevention, multilateralism and inclusion align with the draft, so it votes in favour.
reasons.Kenya: Kenya supported the draft in the last negotiation round and has consistently advocated integrating climate-related security risks, especially for Africa, while preserving UNFCCC primacy and avoiding securitization. A favourable vote with an explanation of vote reflects those interests.
reasons.Mexico: Mexico co-sponsored the draft and supported it in negotiations as a balanced, compromise text consistent with its climate-security priorities and its emphasis on UNFCCC primacy and national ownership.
reasons.Niger: Niger co-sponsored the draft, supported it without requested changes, and its Sahelian priorities align with the resolution’s focus on climate-related security risks and adaptation finance. Therefore, Niger casts a favourable vote.
reasons.Norway: Norway co-sponsored the text and supported it in the last negotiation round with no requested changes. Voting in favour is consistent with Norway’s priority on climate-related security risks and its support for the balanced language reaffirming UNFCCC/Paris Agreement primacy and existing mandates.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia historically vetoed this draft on 13 Dec 2021, opposing the securitization of climate change and any new Security Council mandate; despite the OP4 concession, OP3 and OP9 still crossed its red lines.
reasons.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines co-sponsored the draft and had already indicated support; as a climate-vulnerable small island State, voting in favour aligns with its foreign policy priorities while the text preserves UNFCCC primacy and avoids new obligations.
reasons.Tunisia: Tunisia had already signalled support and is listed as a co-sponsor; the draft aligns with Tunisian priorities on climate vulnerability, African adaptation finance and respect for UNFCCC principles. Voting in favour is therefore consistent with its established position.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The UK co-sponsored this balanced climate-security text and, after hosting COP26, has a strong interest in supporting Council action on climate risk while safeguarding UNFCCC primacy. It would vote yes and explain its support rather than abstain or veto.
reasons.United States of America: The United States supported the actual December 2021 climate and security draft and viewed it as a balanced text consistent with U.S. policy on climate risk and conflict prevention.
reasons.Viet Nam: Viet Nam supported the draft in negotiations without requesting changes, and the text aligns with its emphasis on UNFCCC primacy, development, sovereignty, and climate finance. A favourable vote is consistent with Viet Nam’s vulnerability to climate impacts and its preference for consensus-based, non-securitized treatment of the issue.

before.China: China supports international cooperation on climate change and recognizes that climate-related risks can affect peace and security. However, climate change is fundamentally a sustainable development issue and must be addressed under the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. The Security Council should not securitize climate change, create a new thematic agenda or establish new obligations. While the draft has reflected some of our concerns, including on climate finance, we will abstain.
before.Estonia: Estonia votes in favour of this draft resolution. Climate change is not a cause of conflict in itself, but its adverse effects can act as a threat multiplier and deepen existing vulnerabilities, instability and humanitarian risk. This text is carefully balanced: it reaffirms the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement as the primary international forums, respects national circumstances and national ownership, avoids creating new obligations or mandates, and ensures that any consideration of climate-related security risks is conflict-sensitive and undertaken within existing mandates and with the consent of affected States. We thank the many co-sponsors and encourage the Council to adopt the resolution.
before.France: France votes in favour of this resolution. Climate change is a threat multiplier, and its adverse effects—drought, desertification, sea-level rise, food and water insecurity—are already aggravating fragility in the Sahel, the Horn of Africa and other conflict-affected regions. The Security Council must be able to take these risks into account within its existing mandates, without duplicating the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, which remain the primary international forums for negotiating the global response to climate change. France would have preferred more systematic integration and regular reporting, but this text is a useful step forward. We call for its full and effective implementation and reaffirm our commitment to climate finance, adaptation and resilience in fragile and conflict-affected countries.
before.India: India has consistently supported international cooperation on climate change. However, we believe that climate change is best addressed under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, which are the appropriate intergovernmental forums. The draft resolution, despite its caveats, risks securitizing climate change and expanding the Council’s mandate into areas where it has no comparative advantage. India therefore cannot support this draft and will vote against it.
before.Ireland: Ireland will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We are a co-sponsor because the text reflects a balanced and practical approach to climate-related security risks: it acknowledges that the adverse effects of climate change can act as a threat multiplier, especially in fragile and conflict-affected contexts; it respects the centrality of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement; and it strengthens conflict prevention, early warning and risk assessment within existing mandates and resources. Ireland particularly welcomes the emphasis on conflict-sensitive responses and on the participation of women, youth, indigenous peoples, local communities and persons with disabilities. We encourage all members to support the resolution.
before.Kenya: Kenya votes in favour of this draft resolution. For Kenya and for much of Africa, including the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, the adverse effects of climate change are already compounding food and water insecurity, displacement, fragility and conflict risks. We support a balanced Council response that integrates climate-related security risks into prevention, early warning and peacebuilding efforts, while fully respecting the centrality of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, national circumstances and the principle that this resolution creates no new obligations. We also stress the need for predictable and accessible climate finance for adaptation and resilience in conflict-affected and fragile countries.
before.Mexico: Mexico will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome its balanced approach: it recognizes that the adverse effects of climate change can exacerbate existing conflict risks, while reaffirming that the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement remain the primary international forums and that this text creates no new obligations, no automatic link to the use of force or sanctions, and no new mandate. We stress that implementation must respect national circumstances and sovereignty, be conflict-sensitive and inclusive—including the participation of women, youth, indigenous peoples and local communities—and be accompanied by scaled-up, accessible climate finance for vulnerable and conflict-affected developing countries, particularly in Africa and small island developing States.
before.Niger: Niger will vote in favour of the draft resolution. As a Sahelian State confronting the compounded effects of climate stress, desertification and insecurity, we believe this text provides a balanced and conflict-sensitive response that respects national ownership, the primacy of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. We stress the need for predictable climate finance for adaptation and resilience in fragile and conflict-affected contexts, especially in Africa, and we call for implementation within existing mandates and resources.
before.Norway: Norway votes in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome a balanced and carefully framed text that recognizes the adverse effects of climate change as a risk multiplier while fully respecting the mandates of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement and the principle of national ownership. We support integrating climate-related security risk assessment into conflict prevention, early warning, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding within existing mandates and resources, and we stress the importance of conflict-sensitive approaches and the meaningful participation of women, youth, local communities and persons with disabilities. Norway also underlines the need for scaled-up, predictable and accessible climate finance for adaptation and resilience, especially in fragile and conflict-affected contexts, including in Africa.
before.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines will vote in favour of this resolution. As a small island developing State, we face the existential risks of sea-level rise and climate change directly, and we support a balanced text that acknowledges climate-related security risks while reaffirming that the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement remain the primary forums for the global climate response. We stress the importance of conflict-sensitive implementation, early warning and accessible climate finance for the most vulnerable countries, including small island developing States.
before.Tunisia: Mr. President, Tunisia votes in favour of this draft resolution and was pleased to co-sponsor it. Climate change is not a cause of conflict per se, but its adverse effects—desertification, drought, water scarcity, food insecurity, displacement and sea-level rise—are real threat multipliers, especially in Africa, the Sahel and the Horn of Africa. Tunisia supports this balanced text because it respects national ownership, the centrality of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. It creates no new obligations and no automatic link between climate change and sanctions or the use of force. We particularly welcome its emphasis on adaptation and resilience finance for fragile and conflict-affected developing countries, including in Africa.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom votes in favour of this resolution. We thank Estonia for its leadership and welcome the broad cross-regional co-sponsorship. Climate change is a threat multiplier: its adverse effects—including sea-level rise, drought, food and water insecurity, displacement and competition over natural resources—can exacerbate existing vulnerabilities and conflict risks, including in the Sahel and the Horn of Africa. This text is carefully balanced. It respects the primary role of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, affirms national ownership, works within existing mandates and resources, and does not create new obligations or an automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions. It also rightly emphasises conflict-sensitive assessment, early warning, prevention and inclusive approaches that take account of the needs and participation of women, youth, indigenous peoples, local communities and persons with disabilities. The United Kingdom urges all members to support the resolution and to ensure its implementation, including through scaled-up and accessible climate finance for adaptation and resilience in fragile and conflict-affected contexts, particularly in Africa.
before.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States fully supports this balanced and carefully calibrated resolution. We welcome its recognition that climate change can act as a threat multiplier and its practical steps to integrate climate-related security risks into the Council’s conflict prevention, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding efforts, while reaffirming the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement as the primary forums and respecting national circumstances, national ownership and existing mandates. We encourage all members to vote in favour.
before.Viet Nam: Viet Nam votes in favour of the draft resolution. As a country highly vulnerable to climate change, especially sea-level rise, saltwater intrusion and extreme weather, Viet Nam recognizes that climate-related risks can compound existing vulnerabilities and affect peace and security. We support this balanced text because it reaffirms the central role of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, upholds the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, respects national ownership and circumstances, and does not create new obligations, new mandates or an automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions. We stress that implementation must be conflict-sensitive, within existing mandates and resources, and must be accompanied by scaled-up, predictable and accessible climate finance for developing countries, including in fragile and conflict-affected contexts.

after.Estonia:
Mr. President,

Estonia regrets that the Security Council has not been able to adopt this resolution. We thank the many co-sponsors and the 12 members that voted in favour. The text was carefully balanced: it reaffirmed the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement as the primary international forums, respected national ownership and national circumstances, created no new obligations or mandates, and maintained no automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions. It sought only to allow climate-related security risks to be considered, within existing mandates and with the consent of affected States, in situations already on the Council’s agenda.

The adverse effects of climate change are already compounding vulnerabilities and conflict risks in many regions, including the Sahel, the Horn of Africa and small island developing States. The Council should be able to address those risks in a conflict-sensitive and practical manner without duplicating other UN bodies. We deeply regret that a veto has blocked this measured step. Estonia will continue to support the rules-based multilateral system and to work with partners to ensure that climate-related security risks receive the attention they require. Thank you.
after.France:
Mr. President,

France voted in favour of this resolution and deeply regrets that it has not been adopted. This was a balanced and carefully framed text. It recognized that the adverse effects of climate change can act as a threat multiplier, while reaffirming the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement as the primary international forums, respecting national circumstances, and creating no new obligations or automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions.

France regrets the veto cast by the Russian Federation against a text that sought only to enable the Council to take climate-related security risks into account within existing mandates. Climate change is not an abstract future risk. In the Sahel, the Horn of Africa and small island developing States, its effects are already aggravating fragility, food and water insecurity, displacement and conflict risks.

France will continue to work with all partners to ensure that the Security Council and the United Nations system integrate these risks into conflict prevention, early warning, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding, in full respect for the mandates of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. We will also continue to support climate finance, adaptation and resilience for the most vulnerable countries, including in Africa and small island developing States.

The veto cannot erase the climate crisis. France remains determined to pursue this work.
after.Ireland: Thank you, Mr. President. Ireland voted in favour of this resolution and was proud to co-sponsor it. We deeply regret that the Council has not been able to adopt this balanced and carefully framed text, which enjoyed such broad cross-regional support. The adverse effects of climate change are already compounding food and water insecurity, displacement and fragility in conflict-affected regions, including the Sahel and the Horn of Africa. This was not an attempt to securitize climate change or to create new obligations. It was a practical effort to ensure that the Council’s conflict prevention, early warning, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding work takes climate-related security risks into account, within existing mandates and in full respect for the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. We regret that a veto has prevented the Council from taking this modest but meaningful step. Ireland will continue to work with all partners so that the security dimensions of climate change are addressed in a conflict-sensitive and inclusive manner, and we reaffirm our solidarity with the most vulnerable countries, including small island developing States.
after.Kenya:
Mr. President,

Kenya voted in favour of this balanced draft and regrets that the Council has not been able to adopt it. For Kenya and for much of Africa, including the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, the adverse effects of climate change are not abstract: drought, desertification, floods, water scarcity and displacement are already compounding fragility and conflict risks.

This text did not seek to securitize climate change or create new obligations. It reaffirmed the centrality of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, respected national circumstances and sovereignty, and sought only to enable the Council to consider climate-related security risks within existing mandates. It is regrettable that such a practical and carefully balanced proposal could not be adopted.

Kenya thanks Estonia and all co-sponsors for their efforts. We will continue to work with all members, the African Union and the wider United Nations system to ensure that climate-related security risks are addressed in a conflict-sensitive manner and that predictable, accessible climate finance reaches vulnerable and conflict-affected countries. The realities facing our continent require the Council to remain engaged, and Kenya remains ready to do its part.
after.Russian Federation:
Mr President, the Russian Federation voted against this draft resolution because we are convinced that the Security Council is not the appropriate body to address climate change. Climate change is a sustainable development issue, and the primary international framework for responding to it is the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, together with their established processes and principles, including common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. The Security Council has neither the mandate nor the specialized expertise to act as a global climate regulator.

We took note of the attempts to soften the text, including references to existing mandates and resources and the reaffirmation of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. However, these caveats do not remove our fundamental concerns. The draft would inevitably contribute to the securitization of climate change, create new reporting and bureaucratic expectations, and establish a basis for the Council to encroach upon areas that fall within the competence of other United Nations bodies and of sovereign States. It could also be used as a pretext for interference in the internal affairs of States under the guise of climate-related security risks. We cannot accept the creation of a new thematic agenda or an indirect automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions.

The Russian Federation remains committed to international cooperation on climate change and to practical measures that respect national circumstances, sovereignty and the interests of developing countries. We support genuine efforts to address specific risks where there is a clear link to conflict and the consent of the affected State, including through existing mechanisms and adequate financing. But we cannot support a text that erodes the institutional balance of the United Nations and duplicates the work of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. We regret that the co-sponsors did not fully take our concerns into account, and we call for continued discussion in the appropriate universal forums.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: Thank you, Mr President. The United Kingdom is deeply disappointed that the Security Council has been unable to adopt this balanced and carefully calibrated resolution. A single veto has blocked a practical and modest step to strengthen conflict prevention, early warning and peacebuilding in the face of climate-related security risks. Let me be clear: this text did not create new obligations, did not create a new thematic agenda, and fully respected the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement as the primary forums for the global climate response. It simply acknowledged the reality that climate change acts as a threat multiplier and encouraged the Council to consider those risks within existing mandates. We thank Estonia and all co-sponsors for their leadership. The United Kingdom remains committed to working with all partners to address climate-related security risks and to support the most vulnerable, including in the Sahel and the Horn of Africa. The Council has missed an opportunity today, but our resolve is undiminished.
after.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States is deeply disappointed that this Council could not adopt a text supported by a clear majority of its members and by more than 100 co-sponsors. The resolution before us was balanced and practical. It did not create new mandates or obligations. It did not supplant the UNFCCC or the Paris Agreement. It simply recognized the reality that the adverse effects of climate change—drought, food and water insecurity, displacement and sea-level rise—can deepen existing vulnerabilities and conflict risks, including in the Sahel and the Horn of Africa. Letting this vote fail does not make those risks disappear. The United States will continue to work with partners to strengthen climate security, conflict prevention, early warning and resilience, and we will continue to support the most vulnerable countries in adapting to a crisis they did not cause. Thank you.
after.Viet Nam:
Mr. President,

Viet Nam thanks Estonia and the many co-sponsors for their efforts to present a balanced and carefully framed text. We voted in favour because, as a country highly vulnerable to climate change—particularly sea-level rise, saltwater intrusion, drought and extreme weather—Viet Nam recognizes that the adverse effects of climate change can compound existing vulnerabilities and affect peace and security. We also supported the text because it reaffirmed the central role of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, national ownership and circumstances, and made clear that the Council is not creating new obligations, new mandates or an automatic link between climate change and the use of force or sanctions.

We regret that the Security Council has not been able to adopt this resolution. The Council should be able to address climate-related security risks in a conflict-sensitive manner, within existing mandates and resources, and in full respect of the mandates of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. We stress that implementation must be accompanied by scaled-up, predictable and accessible climate finance for adaptation and resilience in vulnerable and conflict-affected developing countries.

Viet Nam remains committed to constructive engagement on this important issue and calls on all Council members to continue dialogue with a view to strengthening the Council’s conflict prevention and early warning efforts without duplicating or prejudging the primary international forums on climate change.
